result: Transparent soil microcosms constructed from Nafion and cryolite enable visualization of microbes via fluorescence microscopy and non-destructive measurement of microbial activity via Raman microspectroscopy. Both substrates support high-resolution three-dimensional imaging and are compatible with Raman-based stable isotope probing.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C41, C42, C53, and C54 are well-supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript, including Figures 1-5 showing fluorescence imaging of bacteria and fungi, and Figures 6-7 demonstrating Raman detection of deuterium and 13C uptake in cells within both transparent soil matrices.

result: Both Nafion and cryolite function as optically transparent soil substrates that enable growth, maintenance, and visualization of microbial cells in three dimensions over time, and are compatible with stable isotope probing using Raman spectroscopy.
evaluation: Claims C5-C8, C28, and C31 are supported by experimental demonstrations showing microbial growth in both substrates (Figure 5), imaging through 100 µm depth (Figures 3-4), and Raman detection of isotope-labeled cells (Figures 6-7).

result: Optical characterization using fluorescent beads shows that both Nafion and cryolite enable imaging through 100 µm depth with acceptable resolution loss. Cryolite shows better optical performance than Nafion, with less brightness decay and better resolution preservation with depth.
evaluation: Claims C70-C77 are supported by quantitative measurements in Figure 3, showing statistically significant differences in bead brightness and FWHM at various depths. The data demonstrate approximately 10% resolution loss in Nafion and 5% in cryolite at 100 µm depth, with appropriate statistical tests (ANOVA, Tukey-Kramer HSD, bootstrap tests).

result: B. subtilis bacteria are visible up to approximately 75 µm depth in Nafion and at least 100 µm depth in cryolite. Bacteria are more visible in the PMT channel than fluorescence channels, and in cryolite, bacteria are visible even without fluorescent labeling.
evaluation: Claims C84-C88 are supported by experimental observations in Figure 4 and Videos 1-4. The visibility of bacteria in the PMT channel without fluorescence in cryolite is demonstrated, though the inference about suitability for non-genetically tractable organisms (C89) is speculative.

result: Both B. subtilis bacteria and M. fragilis fungi can be grown and visualized non-destructively over time in both Nafion and cryolite transparent soil microcosms. B. subtilis cells remain active for at least 2 weeks, and M. fragilis spores grow into mycelial masses within 48 hours.
evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing time-course imaging of both bacteria and fungi in both substrates. The biocompatibility and growth dynamics are clearly demonstrated.

result: Both Nafion and cryolite enable measurement of deuterium uptake as a marker of microbial activity using Raman microspectroscopy. D2O-grown cells show significantly larger CD region area than H2O-grown cells in both substrates and on aluminum slides. Single-cell D2O uptake measurements are possible in Nafion.
evaluation: Claims C44, C102-C104, and C166 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6 with appropriate statistical tests (Welch's t-test, bootstrap tests, all p<0.001). The ability to distinguish D2O-labeled from H2O-labeled cells is demonstrated quantitatively.

result: Cryolite-based transparent soil microcosms enable measurement of microbial uptake of 13C-labeled carbon at the population level. 13C-grown cells measured within cryolite have significantly higher Percent 13C values than 12C-grown cells.
evaluation: Claims C45, C117, C118, and C178 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7C showing statistically significant differences between 12C and 13C-labeled cells in cryolite (Welch's t-test p=0.0001348). The low background of cryolite enables this detection.

result: In Nafion transparent soil microcosms, 12C- and 13C-labeled cells cannot be clearly distinguished due to a Nafion-specific peak at 965 cm⁻¹ that interferes with detection of the 13C phenylalanine peak. Nafion may not be ideally suited for microbial carbon-uptake studies.
evaluation: Claims C113-C116 and C176 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7B showing no significant difference between 12C and 13C-labeled cells in Nafion (p=0.2151), and spectral analysis in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1-2 showing the interfering Nafion peak at 965 cm⁻¹.

result: After a desiccation/rehydration cycle, most B. subtilis cells (60-70%) showed no detectable D2O uptake. However, among active cells, those attached to dead M. fragilis hyphae incorporated significantly more D2O than cells far from hyphae, indicating higher metabolic activity near fungal structures.
evaluation: Claims C9, C123, C124, and C126 are supported by experimental data in Figure 8B showing statistically significant differences when replicates are pooled (p=0.01782). However, claim C127 shows that when replicate is added as a factor, neither replicate nor distance category accounts for variance (p=0.2255 and p=0.2248), indicating high inter-replicate variability. The result is uncertain due to this inconsistency and the acknowledged high variability between replicates (C128).

result: The differences between D2O- and H2O-labeled cell populations in transparent soil microcosms are about 10-fold lower than on aluminum slides. Classification thresholds can be established for Nafion (CD=0.5, ~9% false-negative rate) and cryolite (CD=0.75, ~20% false-positive and ~19% false-negative rates). Single-cell deuterium labeling cannot be confidently assigned in cryolite.
evaluation: Claims C105-C110 and C167 are supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data in Figure 6, with clear documentation of false-positive and false-negative rates. The limitation for single-cell assignment in cryolite is appropriately acknowledged based on the high false-positive rate.

result: Exact refractive index matching is not necessary to obtain well-resolved images of 1 µm-diameter fluorescent objects through 100 µm of transparent soil. Micron-sized bacteria can be imaged in both Nafion and cryolite microcosms to considerable depth despite slight RI mismatches.
evaluation: Claims C78, C79, and C29 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing good resolution of 1 µm beads through 100 µm depth despite RI mismatch, and confirmed by bacterial imaging in Figures 4-5. This challenges previous assumptions about the necessity of exact RI matching.

result: Nafion and cryolite have distinct visualization properties. Nafion particles are visible by brightfield/DIC microscopy, can be stained with sulforhodamine, and show slight autofluorescence. Cryolite particles are not visible by brightfield, cannot be stained, show no autofluorescence, but the matrix can be visualized by staining pore water.
evaluation: Claims C55-C65 are supported by experimental observations in Figure 2 and supplementary figures showing the distinct optical and staining properties of both substrates under various imaging conditions.

result: M. fragilis hyphae grown in transparent soil show less variation in width and a more tortuous growth habit than hyphae grown without transparent soil, suggesting possible influence of narrow pore space and touch stimuli on fungal morphology.
evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by experimental observations in Figure 5C. Claim C96 is speculation about the mechanism, but is appropriately qualified and supported by citation to relevant literature (Soufan et al., 2018).

result: The optimal particle size distribution for transparent soil was between 2 µm and 40 µm based on optical properties and interest in imaging microbes. Smaller particle sizes (1-2 µm) may worsen optical resolution due to light scattering.
evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by experimental testing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. Claim C69 is appropriately qualified as speculation about the mechanism behind the observed optimal size range.

result: Both Nafion and cryolite substrates are non-toxic to heterotrophic bacteria and fungi, are inert (not readily decomposed), enable visualization of fluorescent cells through 100 µm depth, and have soil-relevant cation exchange properties.
evaluation: Claims C134-C137 are supported by experimental demonstrations of microbial growth (Figures 4-5), imaging capabilities (Figures 3-4), and citations for cation exchange properties. The inertness is supported by the chemical nature of the materials and lack of observed degradation.

result: Nafion and cryolite have distinct practical advantages and disadvantages. Nafion is commercially available and pure but expensive and requires extensive washing. Cryolite is considerably cheaper, easily ground to desired particle sizes, and requires no pre-treatment, but is sporadically available and may contain impurities.
evaluation: Claims C138-C139 and C143-C147 are supported by knowledge of commercial availability, experimental procedures described in methods, and citation about cryolite impurities (Pauly et al., 1999). These practical considerations are important for method adoption.

result: Cryolite has superior optical transparency allowing bacteria to be resolved through 100 µm without fluorescent labeling, and has more natural dry-down/wet-up behavior than Nafion. Nafion requires surfactants (ethylene glycol or Tween) for rewetting after drying, which can cause cell stress and nutrient contamination.
evaluation: Claims C148-C153 are supported by experimental observations in Figures 2 and 4, experimental procedures, and citations about surfactant effects (Blank et al., 1987; Man et al., 2017; Hallsworth et al., 2003; Nielsen et al., 2016). These represent important practical differences between the substrates.

result: Cryolite appears to induce cell cluster formation in B. subtilis, with cells localizing to particle surfaces forming small clusters rather than filaments. This may be due to cryolite being less hydrophobic than Nafion, in contrast to Nafion's hydrophobic Teflon backbone which may resist bacterial attachment.
evaluation: Claims C162-C163 are supported by experimental observations in Figures 4-5 and Videos 3-4. Claims C161 and C164 are appropriately qualified as speculation about mechanisms, with C164 supported by citation (Moilanen et al., 2007).

result: In transparent soil microcosms, the CD peak cannot be normalized to the CH region due to water background signal and interference from glass and PDMS. However, substantial gains in cell spectrum quality could be made through improvements in spectral analysis, such as nearest-neighbor deblurring or deconvolution-based background removal.
evaluation: Claim C170 is supported by knowledge of water's Raman spectrum and the experimental setup. Claim C171 is supported by citation (Lee et al., 2019). Claims C172-C174 are appropriately qualified as speculation about potential improvements, with C173 supported by citation to relevant methodology (Govil et al., 1993).

result: To obtain three replicate microcosms, approximately eight were initially manufactured due to quality control requirements. Substantial variation exists between cells even within single microcosms, with particle packing being the major cause of heterogeneity between microcosms, affecting liquid flow and cell distributions. Careful manufacturing technique can help mitigate this problem.
evaluation: Claims C200-C201 are supported by experimental descriptions. Claims C205-C207 represent reasonable inferences about sources of variability based on experimental observations and recommendations for improvement based on experience.

result: This is the first study to perform Raman microspectroscopy of cells within a transparent porous matrix, successfully demonstrating the application and combination of light microscopy and Raman microspectroscopy through deep volumes of transparent soil to visualize microbial distributions and measure metabolic states.
evaluation: Claims C46, C131, and C165 assert novelty based on the authors' knowledge of the literature. While the experimental achievements are well-demonstrated, the claim of being 'first' cannot be definitively verified without comprehensive literature review. The technical achievements are supported, but the priority claim is uncertain.

result: Fungi facilitate bacterial survival in fluctuating conditions, with fungal necromass potentially serving as an important ecological niche for B. subtilis in soils. The high percentage of non-active cells after dry-wet cycles demonstrates the stress of such cycles even for soil-adapted bacteria like Bacillus.
evaluation: Claim C10 is inferred from experimental data in Figure 8. Claims C121-C122 and C181 are supported by citations to previous research (Siala and Gray, 1974; Worrich et al., 2017). Claim C182 appropriately notes consistency with previous findings. Claim C186 is a reasonable interpretation of the experimental results showing 60-70% inactive cells.

result: The refractive index of Nafion is 1.35, water is 1.333, and cryolite is 1.339. Cryolite's RI renders it effectively entirely transparent in aqueous solutions due to close matching with water.
evaluation: Claims C22, C23, and C32 are supported by citations (Leis et al., 2005; Lewis, 2007) and established knowledge. Claim C33 is supported by experimental observations and the close RI match to water.

result: After acid washing, Nafion's sulfonyl group becomes negatively charged with a cation exchange capacity of 81 meq per 100 g. Cryolite particles carry negative charge at pH > 1.5 and are predicted to participate in cation exchange in soil pH ranges (3-10). Both substrates have cation-exchange capabilities consistent with natural soils.
evaluation: Claims C154-C158 are supported by citations to previous research (Downie et al., 2012; Kosmulski, 2009; Lindblad and Duroux, 2017; Slessarev et al., 2016). Claim C159 is a reasonable inference based on comparison with clay minerals. Claim C156 for cryolite is appropriately qualified as a prediction based on surface charge properties.
